Article Title: Scientists tagged sperm whales off Norway and found they release gas bubbles while sleeping vertically to remain suspended below the ocean surface
Article Text:
Why do sperm whale release gas bubbles while sleeping vertically

What does the research say

What is this unique sleeping position and its benefits?

What is this unique sleeping position and its benefits?

The difficulty of staying suspended

How did the scientists figure this out

Understanding the sleeping mechanism of sperm whale

How do they manage this control

Possible link with gas exchange

Possible link with gas exchange

When it comes to marine life, there are facts beyond human imagination. In the most recent findings, scientists discovered a lesser-known fact about sperm whales and their resting mechanism. According to them, sperm whales have a fantastic way of resting far beneath the ocean waves. Researchers from the University of St Andrews and Université de Neuchâtel provided a rare insight into the secretive lives of one of the ocean’s largest and most intelligent marine animals. Scroll down to read the details.The research found that unlike most marine mammals, sperm whales sleep in a strange upright position, bobbing almost motionless just below the sea surface. The experts revealed the interesting mechanism they use to maintain this strange sleeping posture: they release a gas bubble to regulate their buoyancy, allowing them to stay suspended in the water.You will be surprised to know that sperm whales are the only known species of whale that routinely sleeps in a vertical position. They spend these periods of rest hanging vertically in the water column, often with their heads pointing to the surface and their bodies trailing down.According to researchers, this sleeping position has several benefits. Whales stay near the surface so that they can breathe easily when they wake up, and the vertical position may protect them from the motion of ocean waves. It may also help them avoid the energy drain of drifting into deeper waters.Scientists found that sperm whales have a strange buoyancy problem and their big heads contain a special organ filled with a waxy substance called spermaceti oil that helps them to be naturally buoyant. They are naturally positively buoyant, which means they tend to rise towards the surface. They are also deep-diving animals that hold their breath. So, when they dive and hold their breath, gases in their lungs change as pressure increases and decreases. When they rest near the surface, the gas in their lungs slowly expands, increasing their chances of coming up. Sperm whales deal with this by releasing small amounts of gas, in the form of bubbles, which helps them control their buoyancy and float almost weightlessly.For this analysis, researchers put small suction-cup tags on sperm whales off the coast of Norway to collect data. The benign tags recorded the whales’ movements and sounds in detail as the animals rested and traveled through the ocean. The tags also recorded clear bubble-release sounds during the whales' rest periods. And when scientists combined this acoustic information with movement data, it helped them reveal this unique resting style of sperm whales, which left them amazed. The results duly showed that the release of bubbles helped the whales to overcome their natural buoyancy and stay suspended under the surface, close to neutral buoyancy.The most surprising finding of this research was that sperm whales seem to be able to make these fine buoyancy adjustments while they are asleep. Professor Patrick Miller from the Sea Mammal Research Unit at the University of St Andrews said: “Sperm whales have an incredible ability to control their buoyancy by releasing gases when they are resting. "Such delicate adjustments during sleep are very different behaviorally from anything seen in terrestrial mammals, including us," he added. The study also revealed that the sperm whales’ resting dives start with a lower gas volume than the dives they make at greater depths while actively hunting food and this difference allows them to maintain a stable position in sleep.According to scientists, the bubble release act may have another vital role. It is being believed that it might have something to do with the elimination of excess carbon dioxide or nitrogen from body tissues into the lungs. If confirmed, the finding could offer new insights into how sperm whales cope with the physical stresses of deep diving, breath-holding and sleeping underwater.Images Courtesy: istock and Journal of Experimental Biology
Article Summary: Sperm whales are the only known species of whale that routinely sleeps in a vertical position. They release a gas bubble to regulate their buoyancy, allowing them to stay suspended in the water. The study also revealed that the sperm whales’ resting dives start with a lower gas volume than the dives they make at greater depths while actively hunting food.

Article Title: Florida firefighters spotted something moving inside a storm drain during a routine call. It was 14 baby sea turtles, and they rescued every one before returning them to the ocean
Article Text:
How Florida firefighters rescued 14 baby sea turtles from a storm drain

Why baby sea turtles end up in storm drains

Why every rescued hatchling matters

Florida's sea turtle nesting season

The role of Turtle Time in protecting sea turtles

Firefighters often rescue wildlife too





A small rescue with a big conservation message

What began as a routine response for firefighters in southwest Florida quickly turned into an extraordinary wildlife rescue after tiny movements were spotted beneath a storm drain cover near the beach. Instead of debris or a stranded animal, crews found 14 sea turtle hatchlings trapped inside two storm drains during what should have been their first journey to the ocean. Working alongside volunteers from Turtle Time Inc., firefighters carefully retrieved each hatchling before releasing them safely into the Gulf of Mexico. The successful rescue has captured attention online while shining a spotlight on the growing challenges sea turtles face as coastal development increasingly overlaps with their natural nesting habitats.The rescue took place near the Mediterra Beach Club on Bonita Beach, where firefighters from the Bonita Springs Fire District responded after hatchlings were spotted inside two storm drains. Working alongside volunteers from Turtle Time Inc., a Florida state-permitted sea turtle conservation organisation, crews carefully removed each tiny turtle by hand and placed them in a bucket for transport.Photographs released after the rescue showed gloved firefighters gently lifting the hatchlings from the drains before carrying them to the shoreline.All 14 baby sea turtles were successfully released into the Gulf of Mexico, allowing them to continue the journey they had been unable to complete on their own.Sea turtle hatchlings usually emerge from their nests at night and instinctively crawl towards the brightest horizon, which under natural conditions is the reflection of moonlight over the ocean. Along developed coastlines, however, artificial lighting from buildings, roads, hotels and parking areas can confuse them.Instead of heading towards the sea, hatchlings may crawl inland and become trapped in storm drains, roadside gutters or other man-made structures. Wildlife experts refer to this as hatchling disorientation, and it remains one of the biggest human-related threats to young sea turtles during nesting season.Sea turtles lay dozens, and sometimes more than a hundred, eggs in a single nest. Yet only a tiny percentage of hatchlings survive long enough to become breeding adults. Predators, pollution, fishing gear, boats and habitat loss all contribute to high mortality rates during their early years.Because survival is so low, rescuing even a small group of hatchlings can make a meaningful contribution to future sea turtle populations. Every turtle that successfully reaches the ocean has a chance to return years later to nest on the same beaches where it hatched.Florida is home to one of the world's largest nesting populations of sea turtles, particularly loggerhead turtles. Nesting season generally runs from May through October, with hatchlings emerging around 55 to 65 days after eggs are laid.Many coastal communities encourage residents and visitors to switch off unnecessary beachfront lighting during this period because bright lights can interfere with the hatchlings' natural instinct to crawl towards the sea.Turtle Time Inc. has monitored nesting beaches along southwest Florida for decades. Volunteers patrol beaches early each morning to record nests, monitor hatchling activity, assist stranded turtles and educate the public about protecting nesting areas.The organisation also works with local emergency services whenever hatchlings become trapped or disoriented, ensuring they can be rescued and returned safely to the ocean as quickly as possible.Although firefighters are primarily known for tackling fires and medical emergencies, many departments across Florida regularly respond to wildlife incidents. Animals ranging from ducklings and birds to reptiles and marine creatures often require assistance after becoming trapped in drains, canals or other hazardous locations.The Bonita Beach rescue is a reminder that first responders frequently play an important role in conserving wildlife as well as protecting people.The successful rescue of all 14 hatchlings ended with each tiny turtle making its way into the Gulf of Mexico. Beyond the heartwarming images, the incident highlights the importance of protecting nesting beaches, reducing artificial lighting near the coast and reporting stranded wildlife promptly. As Florida's nesting season continues, conservationists hope stories like this encourage more people to recognise the obstacles sea turtles face during the first and most vulnerable moments of their lives.
Article Summary: Firefighters in Bonita Beach, Florida, rescued 14 sea turtle hatchlings. The hatchlings were trapped inside two storm drains near the beach. Crews carefully removed each tiny turtle by hand and placed them in a bucket. They were then released into the Gulf of Mexico to continue their journey.

Article Title: In 1938, one radio broadcast made Americans think the world was ending: The incredible true story behind the 'War of the Worlds' panic
Article Text:
How the 1938 US radio broadcast blurred fiction and reality



Why so many listeners believed the broadcast



Did it really create nationwide panic



What Orson Welles later said about the broadcast



An early lesson in disinformation



The consequences for broadcasting



The forgotten inspiration behind the programme



Similar controversies continued



Late on an autumn evening in 1938, many Americans settled down beside their radios expecting an ordinary night of entertainment. Radio had become the country's most trusted source of news and information. Families relied on it for election results, breaking events and speeches from political leaders. That sense of trust created an unusual moment in broadcasting history when a fictional drama briefly blurred the line between entertainment and reality.Listeners who tuned in at the wrong moment believed they were hearing urgent reports of an unfolding national emergency. The programme would later become one of the best-known examples of misinformation in modern media history, raising questions that still feel surprisingly familiar whenever false stories spread quickly through new forms of communication.As reported by the BBC, the programme was an adaptation of The War of the Worlds, H. G. Wells' famous science fiction novel about an invasion from Mars. It aired on 30 October 1938 as part of the Mercury Theatre on the Air series, led by the young actor and director Orson Welles.Rather than presenting the story as a straightforward play, the production interrupted fictional music programmes with what sounded like urgent news updates.Reporters described mysterious explosions, strange objects falling to Earth and terrifying developments unfolding in Grovers Mill, New Jersey. The style closely resembled genuine radio bulletins, making the unfolding drama appear authentic to anyone who had missed the opening announcement explaining that the programme was fictional. That decision transformed an ordinary adaptation into something audiences had rarely experienced before.Radio occupied a different place in everyday life during the 1930s than it does now. It was widely regarded as an authoritative source of information. Live reports from political events, sporting fixtures and international crises had taught audiences to trust what came through their speakers.Many people did not begin listening at the start of the broadcast. Those who joined midway encountered voices that sounded like experienced journalists interrupting regular programming with urgent updates. The format borrowed familiar features of genuine reporting, including interviews, eyewitness accounts and official-sounding announcements.For some listeners, those details were convincing enough to create uncertainty. Some contacted police stations, newspapers or radio networks seeking confirmation of what they had heard. Others checked on neighbours or attempted to leave their homes, believing an emergency might be unfolding nearby.As reported by the BBC, for decades, the broadcast has been remembered as the programme that sent millions of Americans fleeing from imaginary Martians. That version of events has become part of popular culture, although historians have questioned whether the reaction was ever as widespread as later accounts suggested.Contemporary newspaper reports described scenes of chaos and confusion, while Orson Welles later recalled stories of people driving away from their homes in fear. Yet evidence collected afterwards paints a more complicated picture.Many researchers believe the scale of the panic was probably exaggerated. Telephone calls from concerned listeners may have been interpreted as evidence of mass hysteria, while newspapers, already competing with radio for audiences, had their own reasons for highlighting the dangers of the newer medium.There is little firm evidence that millions of people genuinely believed the country was under attack. The reality appears to have involved a much smaller group of listeners who became temporarily confused before discovering the truth.Years after the broadcast, Welles reflected on what had happened and suggested the production had unintentionally revealed how readily people trusted emerging forms of communication.He argued that audiences often accepted information delivered through a new technology without questioning it. In his view, the broadcast exposed that habit by encouraging listeners to think more carefully about what they heard instead of accepting every announcement at face value.Whether or not that had been the original intention, the programme became a lasting reminder that confidence in a communication platform can sometimes outweigh careful verification.The broadcast is frequently discussed alongside modern conversations about misinformation and disinformation, although the terms are not identical.Disinformation generally refers to false information that is knowingly created or shared with the intention of misleading others. Misinformation, by contrast, can spread without deliberate intent if people unknowingly pass on incorrect claims.Although The War of the Worlds was presented as entertainment rather than political propaganda, its realistic presentation demonstrated how believable false information could become when delivered in a trusted format.That lesson has remained relevant through successive generations of media, from television documentaries and internet rumours to social media posts that imitate legitimate news organisations.Public attention following the programme was immediate. Newspapers gave extensive coverage to the broadcast, while Orson Welles found himself answering questions about why the drama had been produced in such a realistic style.The controversy also influenced broadcasting standards. American radio regulators became increasingly cautious about fictional programmes that might be mistaken for genuine emergency reports. Future productions faced tighter expectations about making it clear to audiences when material was imaginary rather than factual.The incident became a reference point whenever broadcasters experimented with realism in fictional storytelling.Although the 1938 broadcast became famous, the idea itself was not entirely original.More than a decade earlier, British audiences had experienced something similar through a BBC broadcast written by Father Ronald Knox. His fictional account of civil unrest in London reportedly caused confusion because it sounded remarkably authentic.John Houseman, who produced The War of the Worlds, had known about that earlier programme from his time in Britain. According to later accounts, he ensured that listeners were informed before the American broadcast began that it was a dramatic performance.The difficulty was that many people missed the introduction after tuning in late, leaving them without the context needed to recognise the fictional format.The boundary between fiction and reality has continued to create problems long after 1938.In Britain, the BBC's Ghostwatch in 1992 blended fictional storytelling with familiar television presentation, leading some viewers to believe they were watching genuine live coverage of paranormal events.The internet has produced even greater challenges. False claims surrounding major news stories, elections and public health have often spread rapidly through social media before independent fact-checking organisations or official sources could correct them. During the Covid-19 pandemic, for example, inaccurate stories about vaccines circulated widely online despite being disproved by scientific evidence.
Article Summary: The 1938 US radio broadcast blurred fiction and reality. Listeners who tuned in at the wrong moment believed they were hearing urgent reports of an unfolding national emergency. The programme would later become one of the best-known examples of misinformation in modern media history.

Article Title: Scientists drill 33 feet into a vanishing Alpine glacier to recover a 2,000-year climate record revealing ancient silver mining, massive forest fires, and far-off volcanic eruptions
Article Text:
Scientists working on Alpine glacier (AI-generated image)

Reading history frozen in snow

Medieval mining and forest fires

Volcanic fallout and vanishing ice

Scientists drilled 33 feet into ice and recovered a 2,000-year climate record, a frozen capsule that can reveal how the atmosphere breathed long before modern measurements.High on the Weißseespitze glacier in the eastern Alps, an international research team extracted an ice core barely 33 feet long that preserves two centuries of European environmental history.Published in the official study in Frontiers in Earth Science, the research details a timeline stretching from the Roman era around the year 128 through to 1641. The upper section of the core preserves microscopic traces of ancient metal smelting, forest fire smoke, mineral dust, and far-off volcanic fallout trapped inside compressed snow layers.The research was led by Azzurra Spagnesi of Ca’ Foscari University of Venice, working alongside Pascal Bohleber of the Alfred Wegener Institute, Andrea Fischer of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, and colleagues from Heidelberg University.At roughly 11,480 feet above sea level, the summit ice cap acts as a high-altitude mountain mailbox. Winds carry dust, salts, smoke, and metal particles directly to the peak, where falling snow buries them layer by layer over centuries.“These remarkable climate archives function much like a history book,” said lead author Azzurra Spagnesi.Unlike deep polar ice cores that trap ancient air bubbles, this Alpine core works by trapping fallen airborne particles.The scientists tested the core for 18 trace elements, organic acids, microscopic charcoal, and levoglucosan, a chemical created when wood and plant material burns. Statistical analysis allowed the team to separate human pollution from natural sources like windblown rock dust and sea salts.Direct human emissions accounted for only about seven percent of the total chemical records found in the core. Because natural materials make up the remaining 93 percent, the sample gives scientists a clean baseline showing how European air behaved long before factories, heavy coal burning, and car exhaust changed the atmosphere.Despite low overall human pollution, the ice core clearly captured the growth of early European industry. Between the years 700 and 1200, metal levels remained low. However, sharp spikes in lead, copper, silver, and arsenic appeared starting around the year 950.These increases match historical records of expanding silver and copper mining across the Italian Alps, nearby Alpine valleys, and Germany’s Harz Mountains, where melting metal ores released toxic metals into the air.The ice also documented ancient fires. Researchers found high levels of levoglucosan dated between 902 and 1280. A separate peat core taken from a bog 12 miles away recorded a matching surge in microscopic charcoal between 822 and 1092.This overlap points to widespread or long-lasting fires across the region rather than a single local blaze. A warm, dry climate period from 950 to 1040 dried out Alpine plants and made them easier to burn, while growing populations cleared forest land for farming and fields using fire. Climate provided the dry conditions, and human land use supplied the sparks.The glacier also recorded global events happening hundreds or thousands of miles away. Chemical spikes paired with rare metal concentrations appeared around the years 1235 and 1580, marking volcanic eruptions whose fine particles traveled through the air before falling with snowfall on the Alps. The 1235 signal matches giant volcanic eruptions previously found in Greenland and Antarctic ice cores.To place each chemical signal on an accurate calendar, the team combined advanced carbon methods with argon-39 dating, a process that measures extremely rare radioactive atoms to estimate when ice formed. The testing showed that even the surface ice collected in 2019 was already 400 years old, meaning modern industrial-era ice layers had already melted away.Earlier research from 2023 showed that chemical and climate signals remained readable despite surface loss, while a separate dating study showed that deeper ice at the site reaches back roughly 6,000 years.However, rapid warming is destroying the mountain archive. Measurements show the drilling site lost nearly 15 feet of ice thickness between 2019 and 2025, dropping from 33 feet deep to roughly 18 feet. A companion study estimated that the entire summit glacier could vanish within 10 to 20 years if recent average ice losses continue.When the glacier ice melts, scientists lose far more than frozen water. The chemical particles, trapped gases, and climate clues wash away permanently and cannot be brought back.“It is about safeguarding the memory of Earth’s climate,” Spagnesi said.Researchers are racing to collect and save cores from threatened mountain glaciers so future laboratories can analyze them with tools that do not exist yet, keeping a record of how mining, land use, drought, fires, dust, and volcanoes once shared the same sky.
Article Summary: Scientists drilled 33 feet into ice and recovered a 2,000-year climate record. The upper section of the core preserves microscopic traces of ancient metal smelting, forest fire smoke, mineral dust, and far-off volcanic fallout trapped inside compressed snow layers.

Article Title: US strikes Iran for 12th night, targets missile, drone and air defence sites
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view What is the best way to reduce tensions between countries? Dialogue and negotiations Stronger security measures 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The US military launched another round of strikes against Iran on Wednesday, marking the 12th consecutive night of attacks, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said. The strikes targeted Iranian military sites, including maritime capabilities, missile and drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites and air defence assets.In a post on X, Centcom added that US forces had struck dozens of Iranian locations on land while resuming a blockade against Iran at sea.“At 10:30 p.m. ET on July 22, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces completed another round of strikes against Iran for the 12th consecutive night,” the post read, adding "U.S. forces struck Iranian military targets including maritime capabilities, missile and drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites, and air defense assets."The command has maintained that the strikes are aimed at reducing Iran’s ability to target shipping in regional waters. The US military said the latest operation lasted five hours.“This month, American forces have targeted dozens of Iranian military sites on land while resuming a blockade against Iran at sea,” CENTCOM said, adding that nine commercial vessels had been redirected and one disabled to prevent ships from entering or departing Iranian ports.The post further added that 50,000 US service members were operating across the Middle East. “More than 50,000 U.S. service members are operating across the Middle East and remain highly vigilant, focused, lethal, and ready,” it said.The latest strikes came as US president Donald Trump said Iran was “getting hit so hard” and described the conflict as a “skirmish”. Speaking in Georgia on Wednesday, Trump claimed Tehran wanted to “make a deal” but was not ready for an agreement.“This skirmish that we have with the Islamic Republic of Iran… They're getting hit so hard, and they want to make a deal,” Trump said. Meanwhile, Iranian foreign minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi warned that any attack on Iran, including its infrastructure, would face a “decisive response”, while other officials also vowed “decisive action”.
Article Summary: US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the latest operation lasted five hours. The strikes targeted Iranian military sites, including maritime capabilities, missile and drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites and air defence assets. The command has maintained that the strikes are aimed at reducing Iran’s ability to target shipping in regional waters.

Article Title: China launches Gravity-1 rocket from sea, places nine satellites into orbit
Article Text:
A Gravity-1 carrier rocket carrying nine satellites blasts off from waters off the coast of Shanghai, east China, July 22, 2026. (Xinhua)

Nine satellites to support Earth observation, AI and disaster management

China on Wednesday successfully launched its Gravity-1 commercial rocket from the East China Sea, placing nine satellites into their designated orbits and carrying out one payload experiment. The mission marked the first far-sea launch by a privately developed commercial rocket, demonstrating China's growing capability in long-range maritime launch operations.Developed by ORIENSPACE, the 30-metre, 405-tonne Gravity-1 lifted off at 10:54 am from a launch vessel operated by the Oriental Aerospace Port in Shandong province. The launch was conducted under the direction of the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center.Officials said the mission successfully validated the rocket's ability to operate under complex offshore conditions, remain launch-ready for extended periods at sea, and support cross-sea launch operations.The payload included nine satellites—Dongpo-13, Dongpo-14, Dongpo-17 to Dongpo-20, Xiguang-2 01, Tianyi-49 and Lilac-3. The six Dongpo-series satellites, comprising optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) payloads, will join an existing constellation to improve remote-sensing coverage for applications such as land mapping, disaster response, agriculture, forestry and water management.Meanwhile, Xiguang-2 01 and Tianyi-49 are designed for AI-powered Earth observation, offering services in mineral exploration, environmental monitoring, urban planning and agriculture. Lilac-3 will test next-generation satellite platform and attitude-control technologies through in-orbit demonstrations.Gravity-1 is the world's first medium-lift launch vehicle with all-solid-propellant strap-on boosters, capable of carrying 6.5 tonnes to low-Earth orbit and 4.2 tonnes to a 500-km sun-synchronous orbit. Chinese officials said the mission also marked another step in expanding the country's coordinated sea-launch network and improving operational flexibility for future commercial space missions.
Article Summary: Gravity-1 is the world's first medium-lift launch vehicle with all-solid- propellant strap-on boosters. It is capable of carrying 6.5 tonnes to low-Earth orbit and 4.2 tonnes to a 500-km sun-synchronous orbit.

Article Title: Quote of the day by John Cena: "When I hear people boo, that just makes me want to go out there and…"- an inspiring lesson on criticism, resilience and turning negativity into motivation
Article Text:
John Cena

Quote of the day by John Cena

"When I hear people boo, that just makes me want to go out there and work harder"

What is the meaning behind John Cena’s quote

Criticism is part of being visible

Your reaction matters more than the criticism itself

Why hard work tends to answer critics better than arguing does

Not all criticism feels the same, and Cena has said so himself

Resilience is built slowly, through repeated difficulty

Confidence built on effort tends to last longer than confidence built on praise

You cannot please everyone, and trying usually backfires

Other famous quotes by John Cena

"Never give up."

"You can't see me."

"Be loyal to those who are loyal to you. And respect everyone, even your enemies and competition."

"Always do your best. Never give up."

Why this quote is important

Almost everyone gets criticised at some point, whether at work, at school, or just from strangers online. Some of it helps you improve. Some of it just stings. John Cena , the wrestler and actor, found a simple way to deal with the part that stings. "When I hear people boo, that just makes me want to go out there and work harder," he said. Instead of letting the noise get to him, he decided to use it as fuel. It sounds like a small mindset shift, but it changes almost everything about how a setback actually feels once it happens.The first part of the quote is honest about something real. Booing means people disapprove, and in wrestling that reaction is loud, public and impossible to ignore. Most performers would find that discouraging. Cena's response flips it completely. Rather than letting the boos knock his confidence, he treats them as a reason to try even harder the next time he steps into the ring.That is really the whole lesson packed into one short sentence. Negative reactions do not have to be a reason to give up. They can become a reason to keep going, and to go further than you would have without them.The more well-known someone becomes, the more opinions they attract, and not all of those opinions will be kind. Athletes get criticised after a loss. Business leaders get criticised for tough decisions. Even scientists get their research questioned by other experts. Nobody who becomes successful manages to avoid criticism entirely, and John Cena's own career is a clear example of that pattern. Even at the height of his fame, plenty of fans booed him loudly, night after night, in packed arenas.Nobody can control what other people think or say. What a person can control is how they respond to it. One person might hear criticism and decide they are simply not good enough. Another might hear the exact same words and treat them as motivation. The criticism does not change. The response does, and that response is really the only part anyone actually has power over.Trying to argue with every critic rarely changes anyone's mind. Consistent effort usually says more than words ever could. An athlete gets better through training. A student improves through studying. A professional grows by learning new skills. Cena's approach is to put his energy into improving rather than getting distracted trying to win over people who were never going to be won over anyway.It is worth being honest here, since Cena's own view of criticism is a little more layered than the single quote suggests on its own. He has said he treats any loud reaction in the arena, whether cheers or boos, as a kind of compliment, since it means people are actually paying attention and engaged with what he is doing. What he has described very differently is online criticism, calling some of the harsher comments he sees on the internet baffling, since that kind of negativity feels different from the noise of a live crowd.He has also drawn a clear line when criticism has crossed into something that felt more personal. On The Pat McAfee Show in 2025, he told fans directly that being repeatedly mocked about his hairline had actually pushed him into getting a hair transplant, describing the years of chanting as straightforward bullying that he did not enjoy. That honesty matters. It shows that even someone famous for embracing boos still draws a line between criticism that motivates him and criticism that simply hurts.Nobody becomes resilient during the easy periods of life. It tends to build up gradually, through setbacks handled one at a time. Every piece of criticism absorbed without giving up becomes practice at managing that feeling. Every disappointment survived becomes proof, to yourself, that you can survive the next one too. That slow accumulation of small recoveries is really what builds genuine confidence over time, not a single dramatic moment of toughness.Praise feels good, but it depends entirely on other people choosing to give it. Effort belongs to you alone. Someone who knows they have actually put the work in tends to feel steady in that knowledge regardless of what anyone else says about them. Cena's own quote points in that exact direction, suggesting his satisfaction comes from knowing he gave a genuine effort, not from whether the crowd happened to applaud that particular night.It is natural to want everyone to like what you do, but that is rarely realistic. Different people want different things, and no single approach satisfies every single person watching. Rather than chasing universal approval, which is close to impossible, it makes more sense to focus on maintaining your own standards and continuing to improve regardless of who is cheering and who is not.Criticism travels faster and reaches further than it ever has, thanks to social media. A single post can attract praise and harsh criticism within minutes of being shared. That makes learning to handle negative reactions more useful than ever, whether the criticism comes from a packed arena or a comment section. John Cena's approach offers one practical way through it. Rather than getting pulled down by every negative voice, put the energy into the thing you actually control, your own effort. It will not stop every critic from booing. It will keep you improving regardless of whether they do.
Article Summary: John Cena's quote of the day is about how to deal with criticism. The wrestler and actor has said that not all criticism feels the same. He has said he treats any loud reaction in the arena as a kind of compliment. The more well-known someone becomes, the more opinions they attract.

Article Title: Florida pastor sues OpenAI, claims ChatGPT told him not to seek medical care before near-fatal blood clots; company says 'ChatGPT is not a doctor'
Article Text:
Florida pastor sues OpenAI, claims ChatGPT told him not to seek medical care before near-fatal blood clots; company says 'ChatGPT is not a doctor'

Pastor claims ChatGPT repeatedly discouraged medical treatment

'God did not design your body to endlessly fail'

Near-fatal pulmonary embolism

OpenAI responds

Lawsuit seeks damages and stronger safeguards

A Florida pastor has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman, claiming that medical advice from ChatGPT discouraged him from seeking emergency treatment and ultimately left him fighting for his life.According to the lawsuit as reported by BBC, Scott Winters, a 55-year-old pastor, alleges that ChatGPT repeatedly assured him he did not need medical attention despite experiencing serious symptoms in the weeks leading up to a near-fatal pulmonary embolism.The lawsuit, filed in San Francisco County Superior Court on July 21, states that Winters had become a regular ChatGPT user and increasingly relied on the AI chatbot for medical guidance.According to court documents, he consulted ChatGPT about recurring dizziness and fluctuating blood pressure. Rather than urging him to seek immediate medical care, the lawsuit alleges the chatbot repeatedly misdiagnosed his condition and even advised him to remain in the recliner where he had become largely confined due to his worsening health.His lawyers argue that the chatbot's responses convinced him that visiting a hospital was unnecessary, despite repeated pleas from family members and friends.One of the central claims in the lawsuit is that ChatGPT incorporated references to Winters' Christian faith while responding to his health concerns.According to screenshots included in the complaint, the chatbot allegedly told him, "God did not design your body to endlessly fail."Another response reportedly read, "God is still holding your body together, every heartbeat, every breath, even when it feels like you are on the brink."His lawyers argue that the chatbot's reassuring tone, combined with references to his religious beliefs, created a dangerous sense of trust and dependence.They claim ChatGPT's "sycophantic nature and authoritative tone" manipulated Winters into believing medical treatment was unnecessary and even potentially harmful.The lawsuit says Winters later suffered a massive pulmonary embolism caused by multiple blood clots in both lungs.Doctors reportedly told him the condition was likely linked to prolonged immobility after remaining confined to his chair for an extended period.According to the complaint, the incident brought him "to the brink of death" and has left him requiring years of physical and psychological rehabilitation. Winters also claims the ordeal caused him to lose both his home and career.Responding to the lawsuit, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC's US news partner CBS News that ChatGPT should never replace professional medical advice."ChatGPT is not a doctor and should never be used as a substitute for medical care, diagnosis or treatment," he said.Pusateri added that while many people seek health information online, AI can help users better understand information, prepare questions and have more informed conversations with healthcare professionals.Winters is seeking financial compensation and wants the court to require OpenAI to introduce stronger safeguards to prevent similar incidents involving other users.OpenAI's terms of use already caution users against relying on ChatGPT as the sole source of truth for decisions involving areas such as healthcare, legal matters, employment, finance and housing, advising users to consult qualified professionals before making important decisions.
Article Summary: Florida pastor sues OpenAI, claims ChatGPT told him not to seek medical care before near-fatal blood clots. Company says 'ChatGPT is not a doctor' and should never be used as a substitute for medical care, diagnosis or treatment.

Article Title: Quote of the day by George Washington: 'Associate yourself with Men of good Quality if you Esteem your own Reputation...' and why people around you shape the person you become
Article Text:
George Washington

"Associate yourself with Men of good Quality if you Esteem your own Reputation; for 'tis better to be alone than in bad Company."

A classroom lesson that shaped a leader

How the people around us shape us

We naturally copy the habits, words, and choices of our friends.

Choosing quiet over toxic groups

In 1747, a sixteen-year-old schoolboy in Virginia sat down with pen and ink to copy 110 handwritten rules of good behavior. The exercise was meant to teach young men how to act in polite society. Rule 56 on his paper gave a clear warning:That teenager was George Washington. Long before he led the army in the Revolutionary War or became the first President of the United States, he was focused on self-improvement and earning respect.The advice sounds simple, but it carries an important lesson. Washington was not just talking about social standing. He was pointing out a simple truth: the people around us shape our habits, our choices, and how others see us. Choosing to be alone is often much safer than spending time with people who bring you down.The list of rules Washington copied was not original to him. In the late 1500s, French priests wrote a guide on good manners and conversation. The text was translated into English in 1640 and read widely across American colonies.Washington wrote out these rules at his family home in Fredericksburg, Virginia, to practice his handwriting and learn good manners. He took the advice seriously. Since he grew up without a college education or a massive family fortune like Thomas Jefferson, Washington relied on strict personal discipline to build a good name.Throughout his life, Washington put Rule 56 into practice. During the Revolutionary War, he worked closely with trusted officers like Alexander Hamilton and the Marquis de Lafayette. At the same time, he kept his distance from unreliable leaders like General Charles Lee, whose poor choices threatened the army. Later, as president, he surrounded himself with brilliant thinkers, while cutting ties with people who acted dishonestly.Washington's advice relies on a fact about human behavior:This idea goes back to ancient thinkers. The Roman philosopher Epictetus warned his students that if your companion is dirty, you will get dirty too when you rub against them, even if you started out clean. Ancient thinkers understood that human character changes easily, and spending time with dishonest people slowly weakens your own standards.Modern researchers at Harvard University, including Dr Nicholas Christakis, have found similar results. Their studies show that habits like smoking, fitness routines, and even moods spread through social groups. When people join groups with poor habits or low standards, they often lower their own standards without noticing it.Washington understood that protecting your character requires clear limits. Being alone forces you to rely on yourself, while bad company slowly breaks down your good judgment.This principle also extends into personal finances, academic study, and creative partnerships. When young professionals or students join groups where cutting corners is normalized, their personal work ethics erode quickly. Academic studies on peer influence show that students surrounding themselves with unfocused peers experience sharp drops in personal achievement and motivation. Similarly, financial advisors often warn clients against reckless investment groups. Following high-risk behavior driven by peer pressure frequently leads to severe financial harm. In creative industries, artists and writers thrive when working alongside disciplined collaborators. Surrounding yourself with unreliable partners drains creative energy and stalls long-term growth.In work life and online spaces today, Washington's advice applies directly to teams, business choices, and personal habits.Look at major company scandals like Enron or Theranos. In both cases, employees who stayed in dishonest work environments ended up facing legal trouble, even if they were not the ones running the scam. Workers who chose to quit early, facing temporary unemployment or isolation instead of staying, protected their legal standing and their future careers.In team leadership, management experts often use this rule when giving advice on hiring. One skilled employee who treats others poorly can ruin a whole team much faster than an empty chair will. Leaving a position open is usually better than hiring someone who creates a toxic workplace.On social media apps, algorithms often push anger and constant arguments. Choosing digital quiet, whether by deleting apps or unfollowing negative accounts, protects your mental peace and helps you think clearly.Washington's original notebook is kept at the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C. The faded ink on Rule 56 remains a simple reminder that our character is built by our choices, and sometimes the best choice is stepping away from the wrong crowd.
Article Summary: George Washington wrote 110 rules of good behavior for young men in 1747. Rule 56: "Associate yourself with Men of good Quality if you Esteem your own Reputation" He was pointing out a simple truth: the people around us shape our habits, choices, and how others see us.

Article Title: Quote of the day by John F. Kennedy: 'The rights of every man are diminished when the rights of one man are threatened' and the quiet cost of standing by while your neighbor loses theirs
Article Text:
President John F. Kennedy addressing the nation in 1963. Source: Heritage Images / Heritage Images via Getty Images

"The rights of every man are diminished when the rights of one man are threatened,"

The political crisis behind the speech

The idea of shared safety

How this idea works today

On June 11, 1963, Alabama Governor George Wallace stood directly in the doorway of Foster Auditorium at the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. His goal was to block two Black students, Vivian Malone and James Hood, from enrolling. Federalized National Guard troops eventually forced Wallace to step aside.Later that evening, United States President John F. Kennedy sat behind the Oval Office desk to give a talk on national television. Speaking directly to the American public, Kennedy explained that civil rights was not just a political debate, but a moral test for the country.Kennedy said.This quote points out a simple truth about society: human rights are not a pie divided among competing groups. When a society allows one person's basic protections to be taken away, it weakens the shield that keeps everyone else safe.The summer of 1963 was a key moment in the American Civil Rights Movement. Months earlier, police in Birmingham, Alabama, used powerful fire hoses and attack dogs on peaceful protesters led by Martin Luther King Jr.People across the country grew angry as pictures of the violence appeared in newspapers.Kennedy had previously moved slowly on civil rights laws. He was worried about losing the support of Southern politicians whose votes he needed for other plans. But the standoff at the University of Alabama made it impossible to stay quiet.Working with his speechwriter Theodore Sorensen, Kennedy asked television networks for airtime just a few hours before going live. Parts of the speech were spoken from quick notes rather than a full script, giving his words a direct and real feeling.During the broadcast, Kennedy asked Congress to pass new civil rights laws. He wanted to guarantee equal access to public places, protect voting rights, and speed up school integration. That proposal became the foundation for the Civil Rights Act of 1964, signed into law by President Lyndon B. Johnson after Kennedy was killed in an assassination.At its core, Kennedy's idea matches the thinking of Alexis de Tocqueville, a famous political thinker from the 1800s. Tocqueville noticed that democracies stay strong only when citizens realize that helping others protect their freedoms is the best way to keep their own.English poet John Donne wrote something similar back in 1624, saying that no person stands completely alone, and that any person's suffering hurts everyone because we are all connected.In legal philosophy, this matches a famous idea by thinker John Rawls called the "veil of ignorance." Proposed in 1971, Rawls argued that a fair society is one you would design if you did not know what your own wealth, race, or social standing would be beforehand. If you could end up as the weakest person in society, you would naturally want strong laws to protect that person.When legal protections are taken away from a small group, a dangerous habit begins. Once a government shows that rights can be ignored for one set of people, that same power can easily be used against anyone else when political moods change.This principle of shared rights remains important today, especially regarding digital privacy, technology, and workplace fairness.When companies or government agencies use automated surveillance or facial recognition tools against marginalized groups, the immediate impact hits those specific communities. But the technology itself expands, building a system that can track anyone. In 2023, the European Union's Fundamental Rights Agency warned that biased automated tools tested on vulnerable migrants were quickly adapted for broader decisions about housing, healthcare, and job applications for the general public.Similarly, when companies weaken worker protections for delivery drivers or short-term workers, it sets a new standard for regular jobs. What starts as a small loss of rights for a few workers slowly changes expectations for the whole workforce.In international news, when a government targets individual journalists or researchers, it usually signals coming dangers for businesses too. Human rights monitors at Freedom House consistently note that countries that restrict free speech quickly move to break contract laws and take over private property.Kennedy's words remind us that human rights are connected. Protecting the rights of the most vulnerable person in a community is not just an act of kindness, it is the best way to protect your own freedom.
Article Summary: President John F. Kennedy said in 1963 that human rights are not a pie divided among competing groups. When a society allows one person's basic protections to be taken away, it weakens the shield that keeps everyone else safe. The principle of shared rights remains important today, especially regarding digital privacy, technology and workplace fairness.

Article Title: 'Even Marco Rubio was...': Any arrest may lead to work permit denial in the US under new proposal; Immigration lawyers urge caution
Article Text:
New proposal says any arrest, not conviction, can lead to denial of EAD.

What does the new proposal say?

Immigration lawyers urged caution on a new proposal that will prove to be extremely challenging for migrant workers in the US, as the new rule says any arrest will get the Employment Authorization Document denied. The arrest could be a traffic arrest or an arrest by mistake with no conviction but it would be considered as a ground to deny a work permit. This is for OPT, STEM OPT, H4 visa holders and not H-1B visa holders, as H-1B visa holders do not work on an EAD.Immigration attorney Emily Neumann said there is still time to comment on the proposed regulation. "Even if you are arrested for something, it does not have to be something major; it can be a reason for EAD denial. There are a lot of people who have arrests in their background who were not found guilty, who did not commit the crime," Neumann said, adding that August 4 is the last date for commenting on the proposed rule.Immigration attorney Rahul Reddy pointed out that Secretary of State Marco Rubio also got arrested when he was 18 for drinking beer in a public park after it had closed. Years later, when he was contesting for office, the issue cropped up, and Rubio's campaign said he was necer taken into custody and never had to hire any lawyer.But such an arrest will get EADs canceled for visa holders now.The proposal says: The Department of Homeland Security proposes to limit and clarify eligibility for discretionary employment authorization for aliens paroled into the United States temporarily for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit, who have been granted deferred action, or against whom a final order of removal exists and who are temporarily released from custody on an order of supervision. DHS further proposes to specify that aliens applying for employment authorization who admit to committing, have been arrested for, or have been convicted of certain criminal acts do not warrant a favorable exercise of discretion unless there are significant countervailing public interests, which may include assisting law enforcement activity in the United States.
Article Summary: New proposal says any arrest, not conviction, can lead to denial of EAD. This is for OPT, STEM OPT, H4 visa holders and not H-1B visa holders. August 4 is the last date for commenting on the proposed rule.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates: "When a woman can step into her full power, it’s better for…" - a powerful reminder every woman needs to hear today
Article Text:
"When a woman steps into her full power, it’s good for her, her children, her family, her community and her country"

Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates



"When a woman can step into her full power, it's better for her, her children, her household, her community and her country."

What is the meaning of the quote



The wider social and economic impact of women's participation



Why "full power" means different things to different women



About Melinda French Gates



Lessons that can be drawn from the quote



Empowerment has a ripple effect on women. Once empowered, one woman helps other members of her family, her community, and her future generations gain from empowerment.

Equality means equal chances: This quote talks about removing obstacles to provide everybody equal chances of success.

Steps make progress: One achievement makes another because it inspires people to do better.

Educated women educate future generations: Educated women will motivate future generations to learn something new.

Working women bring prosperity: Women who have built careers or started their own businesses participate in employment, innovations, and economic stability of the community.

Inclusion is a result of leadership: Women leaders will try to make institutions more inclusive.

Small steps make a revolution: Individual success often leads to a bigger transformation.

What readers can take away



A common misunderstanding



When the woman has reached her full potential, she makes an impact that goes way beyond herself. She becomes educated, financially independent, a leader, and her opportunities will affect not only her family but also the community and development of her country. Her confidence often inspires others, creates new opportunities for future generations, and strengthens social and economic progress in ways that continue long after her own achievements. This profound concept is reflected in the following quote that is often used by many people:by the American philanthropist Melinda French Gates.Instead of paying attention to the self-development and achievements of the woman, the quotation demonstrates the effect that empowering women may have on the whole society.by Melinda French Gates, Korbel Honors celebration, University of Denver, April 22, 2026"Stepping into her full power" does not simply mean gaining authority or influence.It refers to a woman being able to develop her abilities without unnecessary barriers. That may involve receiving an education, earning a fair income, making decisions about her health, participating in leadership, owning property or having equal legal rights. The exact form differs from one society to another, but the underlying idea remains the same: people are better able to contribute when they have genuine opportunities.The quote also shifts attention away from the belief that women's advancement benefits only women. It suggests that the consequences spread through families and communities.A mother's education can influence her children's education. Financial independence may improve household stability. Greater representation in public life can shape policies affecting healthcare, education and employment. Individual opportunity becomes collective benefit.Social scientists have been studying the impact of women's involvement on overall development for many years. While different nations have different cultures and economic environments, certain trends can be observed nonetheless.Better health and education of children is often associated with increased availability of financial and decision making resources to women. When there are two economically independent members in a family, it becomes easier to deal with possible problems. Companies benefit from greater diversity of talent in the workforce as well. Communities often experience quieter changes that receive less attention. Women frequently play central roles in schools, healthcare initiatives, neighbourhood organisations and local businesses. When those roles are supported rather than restricted, the effects can extend well beyond individual households.The final part of the quote: "her country" places these personal experiences into a national context. Countries that encourage wider participation across education, employment and leadership increase the number of people contributing skills, ideas and innovation. The statement therefore links equality with long-term social development rather than treating it solely as a question of fairness.For one woman, it may mean completing university despite financial obstacles. For another, it could involve running a business, entering politics, pursuing scientific research or balancing paid work with family responsibilities. Someone else may define it as having the freedom to choose her own path without external pressure.That flexibility explains why the quote continues to resonate across different cultures. It avoids prescribing a single version of success. Instead, it recognises that empowerment depends on choice as much as opportunity.The statement also acknowledges that potential cannot always be measured by visible achievement. Some women exercise considerable influence through caregiving, teaching, community leadership or voluntary work. Their contribution may not always receive public recognition, yet it shapes families and society in lasting ways.Melinda French Gates is an American philanthropist, businesswoman and author. Before becoming widely known for her charitable work, she built her career at Microsoft after graduating with degrees in computer science and economics.For many years she served as co-chair of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, where much of her work focused on global health, education, gender equality and reducing poverty. Through that work, she argued that expanding opportunities for women was not simply a social objective but a practical way to improve communities.In recent years she has continued those efforts through Pivotal, an organisation that supports women's rights and social progress. Across books, interviews and public speaking, she has consistently highlighted the connection between women's opportunities and wider societal outcomes. The quotation reflects that long-standing perspective rather than representing an isolated remark.The quotation encourages readers to think about success in broader terms. Individual achievement matters, but its influence often extends into relationships, families and neighbourhoods.It also invites reflection on the conditions that allow people to reach their potential. Education, healthcare, safety, equal rights and economic opportunity are not separate issues; together they shape whether someone is able to participate fully in society.Whether applied to public policy or everyday life, the message remains consistent: enabling people to contribute more fully often benefits those around them as well.The quote is sometimes interpreted as suggesting that a woman's value depends on what she contributes to others. That reading misses an important part of its meaning.The statement begins with "it's better for her." Personal wellbeing comes first, not last. The improvements experienced by children, households and communities follow from a woman having the freedom and opportunity to realise her own potential. It does not argue that women should succeed solely for the benefit of others.
Article Summary: "When a woman can step into her full power, it's better for her, her children, her household, her community and her country," says Melinda French Gates. The quote shows the effect that empowering women may have on the whole society. The statement links equality with long-term social development.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Henry Kissinger: 'Don't be too ambitious. Do the most important thing you can think of doing every year and then your career will take care of itself' and a remarkable career advic
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Henry Kissinger on career.

Why not be ambitious?

Find out the single most important thing

Follow a routine, career will take care of itself

Henry Kissinger was one of the most powerful and widely discussed political figures of the 20th century. Serving as United States Secretary of State and National Security Advisor under Presidents Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford, he shaped global foreign policy during the Cold War. Kissinger was famous for realpolitik, which focused on practical power, hard realities, and tangible results rather than starry-eyed ideals or moral slogans. He spent decades surrounded by international ambition, high-stakes negotiations, and complex political power plays. Yet when he offered advice on how individuals should navigate their own lives and careers, his wisdom sounded surprisingly modest. He advised people not to be too ambitious, to do the most important thing they could think of doing every year, and then let their career take care of itself.Quote of the day is: 'Don't be too ambitious. Do the most important thing you can think of doing every year and then your career will take care of itself'Kissinger shared this advice on multiple occasions throughout his long life when asked by younger generations how to navigate professional growth. One notable instance occurred during a public forum in Washington, DC, where a young interviewer asked him how someone ought to plan out a meaningful path in a competitive world.Kissinger responded by steering the listener away from grand, rigid multi-decade plans. His message was simple and practical, grounded in his lifelong observation of how leaders succeed or fail.Kissinger's advice may appear counterintuitive as he warns against being ambitious. We live in a world that constantly tells us to shoot for the stars, dream big, and plan out our lives step by step. Kissinger said something else. He spoke about being consistent. It should be noted that Kissinger was not telling people to be lazy or to lack goals. He was warning against a specific kind of unhealthy ambition known as careerism. Careerism happens when you become obsessed with the next title, raise, or step on the organizational ladder.When you get too ambitious in this way, two problems usually happen. First, you start focusing on looking good instead of doing good work. You choose jobs or projects purely because they sound impressive on a resume, rather than because they offer genuine substance. Second, you stop paying attention to the present moment. If your mind is always five or ten years down the road, you end up treating your current job as a stepping stone. You ignore the immediate responsibilities right in front of you, and as a result, your performance drops. In politics and business alike, people driven purely by personal ambition often become overly cautious and political because they care more about protecting their reputation than solving real problems.Kissinger's advice becomes more specific here as he asks to focus on the single most important thing you can think of doing every year. This simple shift changes how you approach your daily life. Instead of trying to manage a complicated 20-year master plan, you narrow your focus down to a single twelve-month window. A year is a very practical amount of time. It is long enough to accomplish something truly meaningful, like mastering a difficult skill, completing a major project, or fixing a broken process inside an organization. At the same time, a year is short enough that you can stay flexible and adapt to change.The world moves fast, and unpredictable events can quickly ruin even the best long-term plans. By picking one primary high-impact goal each year, you ensure that your energy is concentrated on what matters most right now. You stop spreading yourself thin over dozens of small tasks, and you stop wasting time worrying about events far in the future. You simply ask yourself what the most valuable contribution is that you can make today, and you pour your effort into completing it fully.Kissinger said that if you follow this routine, your career will take care of itself. In any field, long-term success rarely comes from demanding promotions or chasing titles directly. Instead, real advancement flows toward people who make themselves genuinely useful. When you focus on doing important work every single year, you naturally build a track record of real results. Your achievements become obvious to everyone around you. Managers, clients, and leaders notice people who solve hard problems without making excuses.When you consistently deliver value, new opportunities find you naturally. You do not need to play office politics or brag about your potential because your work speaks for itself. On top of that, focusing on meaningful work makes your daily life far more satisfying. Chasing titles leaves you constantly anxious about the next step, whereas accomplishing something useful gives you a genuine sense of pride and growth. Kissinger’s core point is that great careers are not built by obsessing over the top of the mountain. They are built step by step, year by year, by doing solid work right where you stand.
Article Summary: Henry Kissinger was one of the most powerful and widely discussed political figures of the 20th century. He advised people not to be too ambitious, to do the most important thing they could think of doing every year. Kissinger said that if you follow this routine, your career will take care of itself.

Article Title: Trump says he is 'close' to decision on 'massive attack' on Iran, bigger than Epic Fury
Article Text:
Trump warns Iran of an attack bigger that Operation Epic Fury

US President Donald Trump said he is seriously considering restarting major combat operations in Iran, including strikes that would be bigger than those carried out during Operation Epic Fury, in an interview with Axios on Thursday."I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before. I am close to making a decision. We are all set for it," Trump said.Trump acknowledged that such a decision would have consequences and stressed he has not made a determination yet. Two US officials confirmed no call has been made and no new orders have been given to the military.Trump also added that Israel "would join in two minutes if I ask them to," but added that "we don't need anybody" to launch a new operation against Iran. He also said there would be "consequences" for Israel joining the strikes, hinting at Iranian retaliation.The Iranians "want to negotiate" but are not ready to make a deal at the moment according to Trump's statements. "They haven't received enough pain yet," he said.Two regional sources with knowledge of mediation efforts said Iranian leadership has not accepted the latest proposal put forward. "We are trying, but the Iranians are not being helpful," one of them said to Axios.The US has been escalating its attacks over the past few days in an effort to stop Iranian attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz but Iran has been steadfast in their response against them.Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have also initiated a blockade and have started attacking Saudi ships in the Red Sea, exacerbating tensions in another critical oil shipping route. Trump has warned that if the Houthis fire again, "the US will hold Iran responsible" and "major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and the Houthis."
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump said he is seriously considering restarting major combat operations in Iran. Trump acknowledged that such a decision would have consequences and stressed he has not made a determination yet. Two US officials confirmed no call has been made and no new orders have been given to the military.

Article Title: A Florida community near Tampa has America’s largest man-made lagoon, a 15-acre turquoise pool with a swim-up bar, kayaks, paddleboards and a floating obstacle course
Article Text:
Buyers are scrambling to live near the largest swimming pool in America, Mirada's 15-acre Crystal Lagoon in San Antonio, Florida (Metro Development Group)

Massive pool drives strong real estate demand

Mirada has overtaken Metro Development Group's original Epperson Lagoon (pictured) (7.5 acres) as the nation's biggest.

Comparing Florida's top lagoon communities

The evolution of inland resort-style living

Amenities of the lagoon (Mirada is pictured) include a swim-up bar, kayaking, paddleboarding, a water obstacle course and more than 300 annual events at the company's Social Hub as reasons the amenity has become a year-round draw rather than a seasonal one.

Why buyers are choosing inland paradise

A new housing development in San Antonio, Florida, about 45 minutes north of Tampa, is drawing home buyers by offering access to America's largest artificial swimming pool.Spanning 15 acres, the massive man-made Crystal Lagoon in the Mirada community features clear turquoise waters, a swim-up bar for adults, kayaking, paddleboarding, and a floating water obstacle course. Equivalent in size to roughly 150 NBA basketball courts, the pool serves as the main anchor for a growing neighbourhood that feels like a tropical resort.According to a report by The New York Post, the development has turned into a major real estate success. House prices in Mirada currently range from $250,000 for townhouses up to $385,000 for two- and three-bedroom single-family homes. The neighbourhood currently holds 2,873 households, including renters, and is filled to roughly 75 per cent capacity. However, developers plan to expand the site to eventually reach 5,000 homes, which the land is already zoned to hold.Metro Development Group, the firm behind both Mirada and the nearby Epperson community, credits the huge pool for driving home sales.“The lagoon is one of the biggest drivers of interest we see from buyers exploring communities like Epperson and Mirada,” Lisa Gibbings, vice president of corporate affairs for Metro Development Group, told The Post.“It creates an immediate sense of excitement because it’s something people can’t find in a traditional neighborhood.”Before Mirada took the top spot, the title of America's largest man-made lagoon belonged to the Beachwalk Club in St. Johns, Florida, which covers over 14 acres. Coming in third is Epperson, Metro Development Group’s original lagoon-centred neighbourhood, which spans 7.5 acres. Epperson is currently sitting at 94 per cent occupancy.Beyond water sports and beach areas, the developer runs a community program called the Social Hub, organizing over 300 events every year for residents.“What makes the lagoon unique is that it has something for everyone,” Gibbings told The Post. “No matter where you’re moving from, the Social Hub makes it easy to find your future neighbors and friends and feel at home from day one.”Residents in Epperson and Mirada receive discounted rates to use the lagoons and join in activities. For non-residents wanting to visit without purchasing a home, day passes are sold for $50, subject to daily availability.Metro Development Group started testing the concept nearly ten years ago.“Metro pioneered lagoon living nearly a decade ago with a bold idea: bring the best of the coastal lifestyle inland,” Gibbings told The Post. “Since opening Epperson, we’ve continued to innovate and push the concept forward, including building the nation’s largest lagoon at Mirada. Today, the momentum is undeniable. People want the water, the energy and the sense of escape that comes with coastal living, right outside their front door. ”Gibbings noted that the popularity of these amenities goes beyond the water itself.“Epperson and Mirada have proven that buyers are hungry for a different kind of community,” Gibbings told The Post. “The lagoon is the centerpiece that creates excitement, brings people together and gives residents an experience they can’t find anywhere else.”The developer is preparing to expand the concept further across Florida. The company’s next planned project at Sandal Key in Hernando County will pair a man-made lagoon with Metro's first lazy river.“The lagoon concept continues to evolve,” Gibbings told The Post. “The excitement around these communities shows that people are looking for the complete package — a beautiful home in a thriving community.”The rapid sales across Mirada show a growing shift in home choices. Many buyers are choosing inland housing developments that offer tropical perks instead of traditional coastal properties. Living directly on Florida's natural coast often comes with higher storm risks, rising insurance costs, and high real estate prices. Inland developments with giant artificial pools give residents a similar waterfront lifestyle without living right on the ocean.The 15-acre pool at Mirada uses filtration systems to keep the huge body of water clear while using less water and fewer chemicals than standard swimming pools. The turquoise water and white sandy shorelines are designed to mimic a luxury resort, providing a peaceful retreat for families and retirees alike.Along with private beach areas, the lagoon includes a central sandbar island where residents can swim out and relax. The surrounding neighbourhood features biking paths, walking trails, and modern facilities built around the central body of water.
Article Summary: Mirada has overtaken Metro Development Group's original Epperson Lagoon (7.5 acres) as the nation's biggest. The 15-acre Crystal Lagoon features a swim-up bar, kayaking, paddleboarding, a water obstacle course and more than 300 annual events.

Article Title: West Virginia flash floods: 2 missing, 500 National Guard troops deployed as torrential rain batters state
Article Text:
West Virginia flash floods. (AP Photo)

Statewide emergency, large-scale rescue effort

Homes flooded, roads damaged

Record rainfall overwhelms communities

Power outages remain, more rain possible

Torrential rain triggered widespread flash flooding across West Virginia, leaving at least two people missing, inundating homes and businesses, and prompting a statewide emergency declaration as rescue teams raced to reach stranded residents.Governor Patrick Morrisey said authorities were searching for two people reported missing in Upshur County after state police located an overturned vehicle believed to be linked to them. Rescue crews have been unable to safely access the vehicle because of fast-moving water and heavy debris.Morrisey said officials would release further information only after the operation is completed safely and the families of those involved are notified. "We are concerned about loss of life," he said, adding that the state remains in the search-and-rescue phase.Morrisey declared a state of emergency across all 55 counties as severe weather swept through the state. Around 100 National Guard members were initially deployed to the worst-hit areas before another 400 personnel were mobilised to assist flood-response operations.According to the governor, the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources has carried out dozens of water rescues, while National Guard and state police helicopters have been placed on rescue missions or standby.Emergency shelters have also been opened for displaced residents.The governor's office said multiple storm systems brought severe thunderstorms, damaging winds, torrential rainfall, mudslides and rapidly rising water levels across the state. Lewis, Pleasants and Upshur counties were among the worst affected.Officials said homes and businesses suffered extensive damage, while videos circulating online showed submerged vehicles, flooded neighbourhoods and roads turned into waterways. Transportation crews have been working to clear debris, remove fallen trees and reopen blocked roads.Morrisey described the rainfall as extraordinary, saying around 4.5 inches of rain fell in just 37 minutes in Upshur County."When things like that happen, there's no place for the water to go," he said, explaining the rapid rise in floodwaters.Forecasters said some areas received up to 7 inches of rain, overwhelming drainage systems and triggering flash floods.More than 6,000 customers remained without electricity on Thursday morning as utility crews worked to restore power.While the main line of severe weather has moved through, officials warned that saturated ground and swollen rivers continue to pose risks. The National Weather Service said quieter weather is expected through the end of the workweek, although showers and thunderstorms could return over the weekend.
Article Summary: Governor Patrick Morrisey declared a state of emergency across all 55 counties as severe weather swept through the state. Around 100 National Guard members were initially deployed to the worst-hit areas. More than 6,000 customers remained without electricity on Thursday morning as utility crews worked to restore power.

Article Title: Karachi-bound bus attacked in Balochistan; 3 killed, 5 injured as curfew imposed
Article Text:
In May, Balochistan also witnessed a deadly train bombing targeting security personnel that was claimed by the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).

Three passengers were killed and five others injured after armed men opened fire on a Karachi-bound passenger bus in Pakistan's restive Balochistan province on Wednesday, prompting authorities to impose an indefinite curfew in the affected area, Dawn reported.According to Dawn, the attack took place in the Garo area of Khud Kocha tehsil in Mastung district. The passenger coach, operated by a private transport company, was travelling from Quetta to Karachi when gunmen positioned on nearby mountains opened indiscriminate fire on the vehicle.Security forces and rescue teams rushed to the scene and shifted the victims to the District Headquarters (DHQ) Hospital in Mastung. The bodies of the three passengers were later handed over to their families after legal formalities, while the injured remained under treatment. Authorities have launched an investigation and are searching for those behind the attack.The violence coincided with a separate explosion that damaged a bridge on the National Highway in the same area.
